title: Two views of explanatory translation
bodyMd:
**Passage A**

A translator of an unfamiliar novel should resist solving every difficulty for the reader. A kinship term, ceremonial object, or abrupt change of register may initially be puzzling because the reader lacks cultural knowledge. Replacing each with a familiar equivalent produces fluency by concealing the distance between the worlds. The resulting text can be easy to read precisely because it no longer asks the reader to encounter what was unfamiliar. There is also a difference between a reader encountering difficulty and a reader being abandoned to it. A translator can provide orientation without deciding in advance that every strange relation must be replaced by a familiar one. The distinction resembles showing a visitor how to enter a building rather than rebuilding the building to resemble the visitor's home. Assistance should make an encounter possible while preserving something of what makes the encounter necessary. Otherwise the apparent generosity of explanation can become a quiet refusal to let the original world remain distinct.

This is not a defense of careless obscurity. Where a sentence is difficult because the translator has misunderstood its grammar, fidelity requires correction. But a difficulty arising from the social relations represented in the novel may be part of what the novel communicates. A brief note can identify the relevant practice without replacing it with a misleading local analogy. The reader should be helped across a distance, not told that there was no distance to cross.

**Passage B**

Preserving unfamiliar words can itself create a false impression. A term entirely ordinary to the original audience may become conspicuously exotic when left untranslated. Readers then attend to it as a special cultural symbol, although the author used it as casually as an everyday household word. Literal retention can therefore change emphasis just as surely as substitution can change reference.

A translator should ask what work the expression performs in the particular scene. If its precise social meaning drives the action, a note or a retained term may be appropriate. If it merely identifies an ordinary object in the background, an unobtrusive translation may better preserve the distribution of attention. No technique guarantees fidelity independently of context. The translator must preserve not only what a text names, but also what it makes its reader notice.
